chunks: From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who is not in a state of wudu (ablution), and rain falls upon him until his head, beard, body, hands, and feet become wet. Does that suffice him for wudu (ablution)? He said: “If he washes with it, then that suffices him.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: This report does not contradict what we have mentioned regarding the obligation of sequence, because the proper understanding of this report is that when rain falls upon a person and he washes his limbs in the order required by wudu (ablution), then it suffices him. But if he were to limit himself merely to the rain falling upon him, without himself washing his limbs, that would not be permissible.

key_terms.أَعْضَاءَهُ: his limbs, the body parts that must be washed in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.التَّرْتِيبِ: the required sequence or order in which the limbs of wudu (ablution) are washed
key_terms.الْمَطَرُ: rainwater, the water falling from the sky used here as a means of purification
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual washing required for certain acts of worship
key_terms.غَسَلَهُ: he washed with it, meaning he actively performed washing rather than merely being wet
key_terms.يُجْزِيهِ: it suffices him, meaning it fulfills the legal requirement

ai.seo_question: Does being soaked by rain count as wudu (ablution) in Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the legal ruling of performing wudu (ablution) using rainwater. It indicates that rainwater can suffice for wudu (ablution) if the person actively washes the required limbs with it, while the compiler clarifies that the prescribed order of wudu (ablution) remains necessary.
